One
card

day. Read the card, then take 1 minute to make notes: four words, one for each rung of the ladder.

Card 1 · A teacher who changed how you think about a subject
A
teacher
who
changed
how
you
think
about
a
subject. You should say:
who the teacher was
what subject they taught
how they taught it
and explain how they changed the way you think about the subject.
1-minute
plan: SET
IT maths teacher, secondary school, age ﬁfteen · ANCHOR
IT “You're not wrong, you're
just early” · WIDEN
IT maths as a wall, then a door · LAND
IT confusion is the ﬁrst step of understanding
Band
7-style
answer
(full,
about
2
minutes):
I'd like to talk about my maths teacher from the last two years of secondary school. I was about ﬁfteen, and I
honestly believed maths was a subject for people who could memorise formulas quickly, which I couldn't. She
taught us in a cramped classroom with a noisy ceiling fan, and she had an odd habit of starting every lesson
with a puzzle instead of a rule. One afternoon I was stuck on a problem about folding paper, and I was close to
giving up. She walked over, tapped my notebook, and said, “You're not wrong, you're just early.” I remember
the smell of chalk dust and how warm my cheeks felt, partly embarrassed and partly relieved. Instead of giving
me the answer, she asked me what I could see, and bit by bit I worked it out myself. Before her class, I treated
maths like a wall I had to climb over. Afterwards it felt more like a locked door, where every attempt, even a
failed one, told me something about the lock. That's quite a diﬀerence, because I stopped being afraid of
getting things wrong. What she taught me, really, is that confusion is just the ﬁrst stage of understanding. I still
use that idea when I learn anything new, from cooking to coding. I never became a mathematician, but I do
enjoy a good puzzle, and I owe that to one patient woman and a very noisy fan.
The
same
moment,
Band
6-style: I want to talk about my maths teacher at secondary school. I was about
ﬁfteen and I thought maths was very hard for me. She always gave us a puzzle at the start of the lesson. One
day I was stuck and she said to me, “You are not wrong, you are just early.” I felt better after that. She did not
tell me the answer. She asked me questions, so I could understand it by myself.
The
same
moment,
Band
8-style: My maths teacher in my ﬁnal years of secondary school turned a subject I
dreaded into one I chased. I was ﬁfteen, convinced I simply wasn't wired for numbers. One sticky afternoon,
with chalk dust hanging in the air and a ceiling fan clattering overhead, I was ready to throw in the towel over a
paper-folding puzzle. She leaned over my notebook and murmured, “You're not wrong, you're just early.” That
single sentence took the sting out of failing, and she coaxed the answer out of me rather than handing it over.
Part
3: How can teachers make diﬃcult subjects more interesting for students? · Do you think technology will
eventually replace teachers in the classroom?

Card 2 · A neighbour who once helped your family
A
neighbour
who
once
helped
your
family. You should say:
who the neighbour was
what they did to help your family
how you and your family felt afterwards
and explain why their help mattered so much to us.
1-minute
plan: SET
IT retired builder, night of heavy rain · ANCHOR
IT “I'll carry her, you hold the umbrella” ·
WIDEN
IT nodding strangers became almost family · LAND
IT kindness only needs someone willing to knock
Band
7-style
answer
(full,
about
2
minutes):
I'd like to talk about a retired builder who lived across the corridor when I was about nine. One night in the rainy
season, my mother became seriously ill with a fever, and my father was working in another city. I was terriﬁed.
The rain was hammering on the metal roof, and the lift was broken, so we couldn't get her downstairs. I
knocked on his door, and he came out in his slippers, took one look at her, and said, “Don't worry about the
taxi, I'll carry her, you just hold the umbrella.” I can still smell the damp stairwell and hear his heavy breathing as
he went down seven ﬂoors with my mother in his arms. I felt panicked, but also strangely safe, because
someone calm had taken charge. She recovered after a few days in hospital, and he even came to visit with a
bag of oranges. Before that night, we only nodded at each other in the corridor. Afterwards, he was practically
part of the family. We ate together on holidays, and he taught me to play chess. What that evening taught me is
that kindness doesn't need planning, it just needs someone willing to knock, or to open a door. These days,
whenever I hear a neighbour in trouble, I think of him, and I go and see if I can help.
The
same
moment,
Band
6-style: I want to talk about my neighbour who lived near us when I was nine. One
night my mother was very sick and my father was away. It was raining and the lift was broken. I was scared. I
knocked on his door and he helped us. He said, “Don't worry about the taxi, I will carry her.” He carried her
down the stairs. I felt scared but also safe. After that night we were close like a family.
The
same
moment,
Band
8-style: When I was nine, a retired builder across the corridor eﬀectively rescued my
family. My mother's fever spiked in the middle of a downpour, my father was in another city, and the lift was
dead. Heart pounding, I hammered on his door. He emerged in slippers, took one look and said, “Forget the
taxi, I'll carry her.” Seven ﬂights, rain drumming on the roof, his breath heavy in the damp stairwell: I held the
umbrella and felt panic give way to something steadier.
Part
3: Why do people in big cities often not know their neighbours? · Is it the responsibility of individuals or of
the government to help people in an emergency?

Card 3 · A friend who is good at fixing things
A
friend
who
is
good
at
ﬁxing
things. You should say:
who your friend is
what kinds of things they ﬁx
how they learned or why they enjoy it
and say how you feel about their talent.
1-minute
plan: SET
IT university friend, garage workshop, engineering · ANCHOR
IT “Give me ten minutes and
a screwdriver” · WIDEN
IT I threw things away, now I try · LAND
IT patience, and look closely before acting
Band
7-style
answer
(full,
about
2
minutes):
I'd like to describe a friend I met at university, who's remarkably good at ﬁxing things. He studied engineering,
but his real classroom was a tiny workshop in his family's garage, full of old radios and bicycle parts. The ﬁrst
time I really noticed his talent was when my laptop charger stopped working just before an important deadline. I
was close to panic, but he just shrugged and said, “Give me ten minutes and a screwdriver.” I watched him
open it up, and the sharp smell of hot solder ﬁlled the room. Ten minutes later, it was humming again, and he
refused to take anything for it except a cup of tea. I felt amazed, and honestly a little envious. Before I knew
him, I used to throw away anything that stopped working, and I assumed repairs were only for experts. Now,
I'm much more willing to open things up and look inside, even if I don't always succeed. He once told me that
most broken objects are only broken in one small place, which I think is true of problems in general. He's taught
me patience, and the habit of looking carefully before I act. I'm not as skilled as he is, of course, but I did mend
my own bicycle brakes last month, and I was rather proud of myself afterwards.
The
same
moment,
Band
6-style: My friend is very good at ﬁxing things. I met him at university. He studied
engineering and he has a small workshop in his garage. One day my laptop charger was broken and I had a
deadline. I was worried. He said, “Give me ten minutes and a screwdriver.” He opened it and there was a hot
smell. After ten minutes it worked again. I was very surprised and a little jealous because I can't do this.
The
same
moment,
Band
8-style: My friend from university has an almost uncanny knack for resurrecting
broken things. He studied engineering, but his real education took place in a cluttered garage workshop. The
night my laptop charger died, hours before a deadline, I was in a cold sweat. He merely shrugged, “Give me ten
minutes and a screwdriver,” and the sharp tang of hot solder soon ﬁlled the room. Ten minutes later it was
humming. He wouldn't accept anything but tea, and I was left equally astonished and quietly envious.
Part
3: Why do you think fewer people repair things nowadays than in the past? · Should schools teach
practical skills such as basic repairs as well as academic subjects?
